item.title: McMahon makes another move in cutting red tape as teachers are 'strangled by regulation'
item.description: First on Fox: Linda McMahon backs the Let Teachers Teach Coalition to bypass bureaucracy and empower educators to drive change at local school boards.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX — U.S. Department of Education Secretary Linda McMahon is pushing forward with the administration's campaign to scale back federal education red tape, backing a national movement designed to bypass administrative bureaucracy and teachers unions.

The initiative, dubbed the Let Teachers Teach Coalition, aims to empower local educators and return decision-making authority to classrooms and school districts nationwide.

This coalition was launched on Thursday, Constitution Day, to strengthen civics and history education and "put teachers, parents, and students back at the center of America’s classrooms."

POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ

"Teachers dedicate their lives to the success and well-being of America’s children," McMahon told Fox News Digital. 

"Yet too often, their ability to do that work is constrained by bureaucracy, political agendas, and mandates that have little to do with helping students succeed," she added. "The Let Teachers Teach Coalition is giving a voice to the educators who have spent too long navigating unnecessary regulations and restrictive systems. When we give teachers the freedom to focus on teaching, we create an environment where students, families, and communities can thrive and succeed."

Spearheaded by the the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), the coalition provides educators and parents with toolkits to navigate local school board politics and directly engage board members. The goal is to equip current, former and retired teachers, along with administrators and parents, to drive policy shifts at the grassroots level.

"While some education policy is decided at the state and federal levels, many of the issues teachers face every day are determined by local school boards and districts," AFPI announced in a statement. "Let Teachers Teach will build a national network of educators and equip them to drive change from the classroom up — identifying problems, advocating for solutions, and turning successful local policies into models that can be replicated across the country."

MCMAHON TELLS HOUSE PANEL TRUMP ADMIN MOVING TO DISMANTLE ‘FAILED’ $3T EDUCATION BUREAUCRACY

The coalition aligns directly with McMahon’s primary mandate from President Donald Trump: dismantling the traditional footprint of the federal Department of Education and returning governance directly to the states.

Department officials recently pointed to national test scores showing that only three in 10 students are proficient in math and reading — despite more than $3 trillion in federal taxpayer money spent since the department's creation in 1979.

The movement coincides with McMahon’s ongoing 50-state "Returning Education to the States" tour and targeted local radio outreach, where she has been speaking directly with families about how K-12 schooling will look under the administration's decentralization plan.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS HEAD START BUREAUCRACY IN MOVE ADVOCATES SAY PUTS PARENTS IN THE DRIVER'S SEAT

To facilitate the wind-down of federal oversight, the administration has rolled out interagency agreements — including shifting student loan collection and management operations over to the Department of the Treasury. The administration is also championing the Education Freedom Tax Credit, set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, which will allow individuals to receive a tax credit up to $1,700 for contributions to approved scholarship-granting organizations.

McMahon has repeatedly emphasized that the U.S. Department of Education does not set local curricula, buy textbooks, or hire teachers, describing the agency's primary administrative function as a "pass-through" for federal funding.

item.title: Erdogan's Turkey cracks down on LGBT community in name of preserving family values
item.description: Turkey reportedly arrested some 160 people and blocked 180 social media accounts in a sweeping crackdown on LGBT rights organizations across 15 provinces.
item.content:encoded:
Turkish authorities launched an unprecedented crackdown on the country’s LGBT community on Sunday, raiding gay bars and shutting down activist organizations, in what the government said are efforts to protect Turkey’s family values.

Since the nationwide crackdowns began, Turkish authorities have arrested and detained some 116 people across 15 provinces in actions against LGBT rights organizations and activists. The Turkish criminal justice system has also launched investigations of more than 160 people, according to Amnesty International.

Amnesty International reported that 180 social media accounts belonging to LGBT organizations, activists, journalists and media outlets have been blocked or restricted.

TURKEY’S NATO ROLE UNDER SCRUTINY AMID NEW REPORT ON HAMAS, MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

"This appalling escalation in Türkiye’s crackdown amounts to a full-scale assault on LGBTI rights and those who defend them. The relentless raids, arrests and demonization of LGBTI people under the spurious guise of ‘protecting the families’ demonstrates why defending LGBTI rights in Türkiye is more important than ever," Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said in a statement.

In a statement posted on X, Turkey’s Minister of Justice, Akın Gürlek, said, "we are steadfastly continuing our efforts to protect the family, our children and our youth from all forms of exploitation, obscenity, crime and harmful content."

Gürlek stated that the Ministry of Justice sent a comprehensive directive to the 175 chief public prosecutor's offices in all of Turkey’s 81 provinces to go after content and behavior that the government considers opposed to "public morality" and harmful to the country’s youth.

"The best interests of our children are not open to debate for us. We will show no tolerance for any criminal organization targeting the institution of the family, the future of our youth, and the order of our society," Gürlek’s statement went on to say.

WHO IS TURKEY'S RECEP TAYYIP ERDOĞAN? HOW NATO'S MOST UNPREDICTABLE LEADER KEEPS REINVENTING HIMSELF

Turkey’s focus on family values and traditional norms is part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Decade of Family and Population vision, a long-term strategy aimed at tracking population trends and promote an increased fertility rate to spur population growth.

Many see Erdoğan’s renewed emphasis on "family values" and his targeting of groups he portrays as threats to those values as as an effort to cement his legacy.

An enduring question asked by analysts is as Erdogan ages and approaches another election in 2028 is what kind of Turkey he leaves behind.

"Erdoğan’s "family values" agenda is about more than defending conservative values, it is about defining what kind of society Turkey should be and who belongs in it," Gonul Tol, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital.

"The LGBT community is a particularly useful target because Erdoğan can portray it simultaneously as a threat to the traditional family, a Western import, and a symbol of the cultural values he says his movement is fighting against," Gonul added.

With protests against the moves beginning to take shape, the crackdowns show no signs of letting up, even as international attention and condemnation begins to pour in.

TRUMP BETS ON FORMER NATO TROUBLEMAKER AS TURKEY'S STRATEGIC VALUE SURGES

Police used pepper spray against peaceful protesters in İzmir, along Turkey’s Aegean coast, and detained more than 95 people on Tuesday who had gathered outside İstanbul Courthouse in protest.

Turkey, which officially became a candidate for the European Union in 1999, received strong pushback from the commission.

A European Commission spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Commission is concerned about the recent arrests and legal proceedings initiated against LGBTIQ+ activists, human rights associations, and businesses, as well as of the blockages of websites and social media accounts, accompanied with allegations concerning funding of civil society organizations. We are following developments closely." 

The Commission reiterated that Turkey, as an EU candidate and member of the Council of Europe, should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, regardless of gender or sexual identity.

A spokesman for the Turkish embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.

item.title: Caitlin Clark opens up on conversations with referees as she looks to avoid suspension for technical fouls
item.description: Caitlin Clark reveals how she now warns WNBA referees about her seven technical fouls, adjusting her approach to avoid a one-game suspension.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark says she has adopted a new approach to her conversations with WNBA referees as she attempts to avoid a suspension during the Indiana Fever’s final stretch of the regular season.

Clark has accumulated seven technical fouls, leaving her one away from an automatic one-game suspension. With four regular-season games remaining, the Fever star said she now tries to remind officials that she wants to work with them when discussing calls.

"I feel like the refs might also know I have seven technical fouls, so I always try to warn them," Clark said. "Like, ‘I’m working with you. I’m working with you. Like, let’s have a conversation.’"

CAITLIN CLARK DROPS F-BOMBS AT OFFICIAL WHILE ARGUING FEVER WEREN'T GETTING THE SAME WHISTLE AS VALKYRIES

The adjustment, Clark said, has changed her interaction with with referees.

"I think it’s made my conversations with them more positive and more conversational in both ways for them and for me," she said.

"I mean, I think it’s certainly been, like, a conscious effort about it, and I think it’s helped me play better basketball. It’s just, like, focus on what I need to focus on, and let the last play go. Like, you can’t go back in time and change things."

Under WNBA rules, a player or coach receives an automatic one-game suspension after being assessed an eighth technical foul during the regular season. An additional suspension is imposed for every two technical fouls after that, while the totals reset for the playoffs.

Clark briefly appeared to reach the eight-technical threshold during an Aug. 8 victory over the Chicago Sky. She was called for a technical after making contact with an official while going out of bounds, but the league rescinded it after the game, returning her total to seven and eliminating the suspension.

Clark now has four regular-season games left to navigate. However, she noted that she effectively needs to avoid another technical only during the first three. A technical during Indiana’s finale would not remove her from that game, and there would be no subsequent regular-season contest for which she could be suspended before the total resets.

"I really only have three more games to go because the fourth game starts — if I get a technical, I’m not kicked out of the game — and then it resets for the playoffs," Clark said.

She added that the new interactions have made her "proud of herself."

"I'm really proud of myself, but still three games to go. And I think it's helped me learn a lot about myself and the ways that I can impact my team, and, you know, how to communicate with the refs," Clark said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Clark’s interactions with officials have drawn attention throughout her WNBA career. She has frequently expressed frustration over calls and the physical defense used against her, occasionally directing animated reactions toward referees. Clark received six technical fouls in each of her first two WNBA seasons, finishing one short of the league’s previous seven-technical suspension threshold both years.

CAITLIN CLARK CALLS OUT REFEREES FOR FAILING TO CALL FOUL ON PLAY SHE SAYS GAVE HER A CONTUSION

She has also acknowledged that her emotions can work against her. During her rookie season, Clark said she needed to do a better job of controlling her reactions because her team relied on her to remain on the court. That balancing act has continued as she has tried to preserve the intensity that defines her game without allowing disputes with officials to become a distraction.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

The Fever return from the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup break Friday against the Toronto Tempo. Indiana will then host the Washington Mystics before finishing the regular season with consecutive games against the Minnesota Lynx.

Indiana entered the break at 26-14 and had already secured a playoff berth, although its final seed remains unsettled. Clark returns to the Fever after helping the United States win the World Cup in Berlin.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Dovie Eisner’s beautiful life inspired a generation of conservative thinkers
item.description: Dovie Eisner, born with a genetic neuromuscular disorder, fought fiercely against assisted suicide and championed the right to life until his death.
item.content:encoded:
I can’t remember the first time I met Dovie Eisner, which is odd given that he always stood out, his small broken body wheelchair-bound with a breathing tube as a result of his being born with a recessive genetic neuromuscular condition called Nemoline Myothapy, but I do remember the last time.

From about 2012 until he slipped into a coma last year, and passed away last week on Sept. 11, Dovie was a central figure in the small world of conservative writing and thinking in New York City. It was a group that, along with myself, included the likes of Karol Markowitz, Sohrab Ahmari, and Armin Rosin. Basically, if you had ever written a right wing op-ed in Gotham, you were a friend of Dovie.

Dovie’s position in this circle was entirely of his own volition. He would seek us out, often one by one, first through social media, then a lunch or dinner carefully choreographed to accommodate his severe disability. I’ve never known anyone so anxious to be on the scene, nor so deserving.

CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH

When Dovie would see a photo of a meet-up he had not attended, he would simply reply, "Why wasn’t I invited?" which became an inside joke for us, summing up all life’s little disappointments.

As a thinker, Dovie was top-notch, and two lights shone brightest in his philosophy: the importance of fairness and the importance of life.

Intellectually, Dovie was a tireless — and I’ll be honest, sometimes even annoying — devil’s advocate, with an extraordinary ability to see the best arguments of all sides.

There you would be, waxing poetic about free speech absolutism, and in his quiet wheeze of a voice, he would start listing off exceptions — as if he had a Black’s Law Dictionary stashed somewhere in his wheelchair.

In retrospect, it is amazing that someone whom life dealt with so unfairly held so dear to his broken breast the ideal that we, us human beings, must always treat others with fairness in mind.

Dovie was just as committed to his undying belief in and fight for life. Not just his, but those of the unborn and others in his own shoes, tempted by the easy out of assisted suicide — a practice he abhorred with every fiber of his being.

CLIMBING EL CAPITAN WHILE NEARLY BLIND: WHY EITAN ARMON REFUSED TO SIT AROUND WAITING FOR A CURE

Writing in the New York Post last year, shortly before his slip into eternity began, Dovie said, "The logic of assisted suicide leads inevitably to the conclusion that those with doctor-approved expiration dates are living lives not worth living. Lives unworthy of life, as the Nazis referred to people with disabilities when they set out to exterminate us with their Aktion T4 program. I’ve heard echoes of that myself — from peers, from rivals, sometimes from myself: I haven’t been suicidal in a good number of years, but I can’t say that about my teens and early 20s."

As stoic and strong as Dovie was, there were late-night texts full of fear and sadness as well. He wouldn’t let you off the hook with platitudes, he literally had no time for that. You couldn’t just say, "Don’t worry, it will be OK," because he knew, and you did too, that it damn well wasn’t going to be.

Those are some of the most frank and cherished conversations I’ve ever had. No artifice, no lies, the cold, bitter reality of life’s cruelty faced head on. Everything was up for grabs, because Dovie demanded it be so.

But also, the presence of God’s love — which Dovie found in every face and facet of the world around him — with a depth one could only envy.

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER SPENT 25 YEARS PRAYING FOR TINSELTOWN, SAYS 'YOU CAN'T HATE THEM'

Every writer and thinker who he blessed with wisdom is better for having known Dovie. When we fight for the disabled in the womb, we fight for Dovie. When we fight against the killing of the light that assisted suicide represents, we fight for Dovie.

Dovie, who loved life so dearly, and lived it so fully.

Often, after a group dinner, the bill would come and someone would say, "Who had five top-shelf bourbons … oh." We would all scrounge to cover Dovie’s excessive bar tab, and we were happy to do it. We would all love to do it just one more time. The kid knew how to live.

The last time I saw Dovie, we were standing on the corner outside the Yale Club in Manhattan, and I was having a smoke as we waited for his special minivan to come get him.

SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

"You know, Dave," he said with thick breath, "all I really want is a beautiful wife and like four kids."

I told him, "I get it, man."

He looked at me and said, "I mean, Stephen Hawking did it."

I nodded, took a drag and said, "Well, how’s your physics?"

Dovie spit out his breathing tube and said, "Stop, don’t make me laugh."

I spent a lot of time trying to make Dovie laugh, time I am so grateful for.

Mark Twain wrote that "Against the assault of laughter, nothing can stand." Dovie was like a philosopher stone, turning brutal suffering into humor and humanity at every turn. He was the toughest guy I ever met, and we will not see his like again.

item.title: Talarico hit with ‘blatant corruption’ allegation over hefty salary from consulting firm, campaign pushes back
item.description: James Talarico drew a hefty salary from MAYA Consulting while overseeing the Texas Education Agency that awarded the firm millions in contracts.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, who has repeatedly accused his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, of corruption, is now facing Republican accusations of "blatant corruption" over consulting work he performed for a progressive firm while serving on the Texas House's influential Public Education Committee. Talarico's campaign has denied the allegation as a "lie."

The Lone Star State's Senate race is entering its final stretch, with Talarico leading Paxton in recent polling. A Republican loss could damage the GOP's chances of retaining its Senate majority.

Paxton has projected confidence that, after emerging from a particularly bitter primary race, Texans will respond to his campaign once they hear his message. Talarico, meanwhile, has continued targeting Paxton through major ad buys, including one in which the Democrat calls him "the most corrupt politician in Texas."

Republicans are now responding with allegations of their own, characterizing Talarico's past arrangement with the consulting firm as a "textbook pay-to-play scheme."

SHOCK POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD

They are pointing to paychecks Talarico received from a firm called MAYA Consulting that simultaneously drew in millions in state contracts awarded by the Texas Education Agency (TEA), which he helped provide oversight to as a member of the Public Education Committee.

Talarico announced he was joining MAYA Consulting in a 2019 Facebook post. In the post, he stated that as a consultant he would be "working with districts, nonprofits, and communities to build excellent and equitable educational opportunities for all our students."

According to a Senate campaign financial disclosure filed in 2025, Talarico worked with MAYA Consulting, which has since been rebranded as VIDA Collaborative, from 2019 until 2025.

During those same years, official legislative records show that Talarico served as a voting member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee from 2019 to 2025. Among its responsibilities, the committee oversees the Texas Education Agency, which awards government contracts to firms for services, including then-MAYA Consulting.

TED CRUZ, CONSERVATIVES RESPOND AFTER TALARICO CRITICIZES BIBLE-RELATED EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS AS 'PROPAGANDA'

TEA registers from 2021 and 2022 show that the agency awarded MAYA two contracts worth $3.578 million and $1.635 million, respectively. The contracts were related to priorities Talarico was pushing in the Texas House at the time, including addressing learning loss due to COVID-19.

Meanwhile, Talarico’s disclosure shows that he earned $83,333.40 from the nonprofit in 2025, in addition to his $13,904.92 part-time salary as a member of the Texas House of Representatives.

Kassi Longoria, CEO of VIDA Collaborative, confirmed with Fox News Digital that Talarico served as an "independent contractor consultant" with the group from 2019 to 2025. She said that Talarico "has no current role with our organization" and clarified that "during his time at VIDA, his consulting work was structured, specifically to remain separate from his role as a Texas state legislator."

She said that Talarico "never worked under, received compensation from, or was involved in securing any state- or federally-funded contracts." She noted that "as a matter of standard practice, VIDA discloses any outside employment or potential conflicts of interest for our staff — including Rep. Talarico’s legislative role — in our proposals when we apply for publicly-funded opportunities" and that "similarly, Rep. Talarico’s relationship with VIDA was disclosed in his required public financial disclosure filings."

However, Republican National Committee spokesman Zach Kraft accused Talarico of wrongdoing, calling the Democrat’s involvement with MAYA an example of "blatant corruption."

TEXAS DEM CANDIDATE TO HOLD HIGH-DOLLAR HOLLYWOOD FUNDRAISER WHILE GOP GATHERS IN DALLAS: 'FAKE COWBOY'

"We are looking at a textbook pay-to-play scheme with James Talarico steering millions in taxpayer funds to his DEI consulting agency under the condition he gets commission through a scam no-show job," Kraft told Fox News Digital.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

As a member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee, Talarico was not involved in TEA's process for awarding outside contracts and did not vote on the contracts. Fox News Digital is also not aware of any evidence that Talarico received a commission for contracts awarded to MAYA, a claim that both the organization and Talarico’s campaign denied.

Kraft alleged that Talarico is "one of the most morally bankrupt individuals to ever run for public office in Texas."

JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, pushed back, saying, "This is a lie."

Ennis said that "James’ relationship to MAYA was fully disclosed in compliance with Texas House rules" and that "James had no involvement in MAYA Consulting securing any public contracts and his contract with MAYA barred him from representing MAYA before the Texas Legislature or education agencies."

"Ken Paxton is making up lies about James to distract from the fact that he’s been impeached by his own party for bribery, reported to the FBI by his own staff, and indicted for investment fraud for scamming his own friends," Ennis alleged, while adding, "Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas, and this November, Republicans, Democrats, and independents will come together to reject Ken Paxton’s corruption and stand up to this broken, corrupt political system."

In July 2015, Paxton was indicted on charges that he misled and defrauded tech startup investors and failed to disclose that the startup was paying him to promote its stock. Prosecutors agreed in 2024 to drop the charges under a deal requiring Paxton to pay about $271,000 in restitution, perform 100 hours of community service and complete 15 hours of legal ethics courses. Paxton did not enter a plea under the agreement and was never convicted.

Meanwhile, Madison Cercy, a spokeswoman for Paxton's campaign, told Fox News Digital, "It couldn’t be clearer: James Talarico sees Texans tax dollars as his own personal slush fund."

Fox News Digital is not aware of any evidence that Talarico has misused tax dollars.

Cercy called Talarico a "taxpayer-funded DEI consultant whose employer receives millions of dollars from Texans while pushing radical ideology in our schools."

item.title: GOP lawmakers pump brakes on Trump's $5K check promise: 'Where are you getting the money?'
item.description: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend check promise faces skepticism on Capitol Hill as key Republicans question its cost and inflation risks.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's promise of a big payout for Americans if Republicans win the midterms is getting a rocky reception on Capitol Hill.

Several Republicans outright oppose the $5,000 check promise, while others offered tacit support in comments to Fox News Digital but hesitated on whether it could actually be delivered. It's a sign that the GOP will have an uphill fight to get the "Trump dividend" approved by Congress with the president and lawmakers divided over whether it even needs the legislative branch's green light.

"I disagree with it. It's pay-to-play," Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., told Fox News Digital. "You shouldn't pay anybody to vote your conscience. Plus, where are you getting the money? I think we're in debt $40 trillion."

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., whose powerful committee would likely play a major role in crafting the $5,000 stimulus if it did run through Congress, said he was "skeptical" it could be achieved.

TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME'

"Take a billion dollars. ... I'd rather use it to either bolster defense or save Social Security. I think that's a better use of the money. But, again, we have to see what we're looking at. Right now, we don't have a bill," Cole told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

He added more optimistically, "We just have an idea that we want to get money back to the American people. I like that."

Rep. John Rutherford, R-Fla., said he could support the idea if the sudden injection of cash wouldn't send inflation rates soaring.

"But it ought to be limited — people that are working, people that are paying taxes. I don't think we should just send paychecks out to everybody willy-nilly," Rutherford told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Beth Van Duyne, R-Texas, simply said, "The devil's always in the details. I prefer to look at ways of getting people job opportunities."

VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS

Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., praised Trump's candor but signaled he was not enthusiastic about a stimulus without guardrails.

"If we can structure tax incentives, if we can do some type of — whether it's a cut, whether it's a rebate, something in that vein, I think it's probably a little better policy than mailing people a check just because they're here," Knott said.

But the idea did find support from others, like House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md.

"I think that hardworking Americans, probably taxpayers, deserve a tax rebate. We’re going to have to discuss how large a rebate that’ll be," Harris told Fox News Digital, suggesting the $5,000 figure should be up for negotiation. "That’s a good idea."

He added that it should go through Congress, potentially through the same mechanism that Republicans used to pass the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.

"It would probably have to go through reconciliation," he said.

Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, suggested the money could come from what the federal government recovers in efforts to crack down on waste, fraud and abuse of taxpayer dollars.

"Why don't we continue the president's approach towards fraud and give a dividend to the people of this great country who that money was stolen from?" Pfluger suggested, arguing that hundreds of billions of dollars were lost to fraud in the last administration.

Giving $5,000 to every American adult could cost at least $1 trillion by some estimates, a significant portion of the U.S. annual budget. A price tag that big historically would be subject to congressional approval, but the president may disagree.

"I think they will do it if we needed it, but I think not," Trump told CBS News when asked if Congress would need to approve the stimulus.

But Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told CNN's "State of the Union" earlier this week, "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act."

item.title: America’s hunters get an exclusive seat at Trump’s White House table as he takes aim at Biden-era rules
item.description: Trump will sign two executive orders at the White House expanding hunting on public lands and offshore recreational fishing before a Rose Garden dinner.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will host more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders for dinner at the White House on Thursday night, where he is expected to sign executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing opportunities and reversing certain Biden-era restrictions.

Trump will deliver remarks to the sportsmen and industry representatives gathered for the dinner in the Rose Garden as his administration moves to open more public lands and waterways, ease regulatory barriers and promote hunting among younger Americans and veterans, Fox News Digital learned.

He is expected to sign a pair of executive orders in the Oval Office Thursday aimed at expanding "America’s public lands and waterways," promoting healthy wild game populations and expanding access to offshore recreational fishing, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP WILL WELCOME FARMERS AND RANCHERS TO WHITE HOUSE DINNER TO CELEBRATE TRADE, TAX WINS

Representatives from organizations and companies including Bass Pro Shops, the Cabela Family Foundation, the National Rifle Association, Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Yamaha Marine Group, Polaris, Beretta USA, Safari Club International, Primos Hunting, Dallas Safari Club, Outdoor Sportsman Group, Sportsmen’s Alliance, USA Shooting Foundation, Ducks Unlimited, Sportsman Boats, Contender Boats, Taurus Holdings and the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation are expected to attend.

America’s outdoor recreation sector generates over $1.2 trillion annually and supports over 5 million jobs, according to a White House official.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and officials from the Commerce Department and NOAA will be present, Fox News Digital learned.

CONGRESS SHOULD HONOR TEDDY ROOSEVELT AND CONSERVE OUR OUTDOORS FOR THE NEXT 250 YEARS

The secretaries of Interior, Agriculture, War and Commerce are directed to propose changes to current policies.

One of the policies spotlighted in the order targets Biden-era restrictions on the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle.

Under Biden, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service adopted station-specific requirements for lead-free ammunition and/or tackle at several national wildlife refuges.

DENNY HAMLIN SAYS FORWARD-FACING SONAR IN PROFESSIONAL BASS FISHING HAS GONE 'A LITTLE OVERBOARD'

Trump’s fishing order seeks to unleash more of America’s coastal waters for recreational fishing while cutting federal red tape and giving anglers a bigger role in how fisheries are managed.

The administration seeks to move charter operators toward multi-year permits, replace mail-in catch surveys with mobile reporting, launch programs for depleted stocks such as Atlantic striped bass, and use eligible offshore oil and gas platforms to create artificial reefs.

item.title: Philadelphia home search uncovers possible human ashes, images of 7 missing women: police
item.description: Ashtrays containing possible human remains and images of seven missing women were found among over 1 million files inside Eugene Horsch's Philadelphia home.
item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia police found images of seven missing women, including two who appear unconscious and injured, while searching more than 1 million images recovered from a home where investigators also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said Wednesday.

Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Armando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said during a news conference.

Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. 

CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS

"Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said. "To date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."

The home belonged to deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch and was occupied by his son, Eugene Horsch, whose June arrest sparked the investigation.

On June 19, a Federal Park Ranger arrested Eugene Horsch, 44, after investigating him and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained.

"During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said.

The female passenger presented police with a false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital.

FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY

The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown.

After obtaining a warrant, investigators found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras and phones," Vanore said during the press conference.

Investigators have identified 58 people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them."

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

One video shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Police identified this woman as Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia.

Another missing woman connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported.

Two other missing women have been connected to the home. Police identified one as a 25-year-old woman but did not name her, and the other has yet to be identified, according to FOX 29.

"We have only processed a small fraction of the total media. Thousands of videos remain to be analyzed. We are working to corroborate what we see and gather physical evidence to prove our findings, supported throughout by the FBI as we determine our next steps," Vanore concluded Wednesday.

item.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker called out by MS NOW hosts in fiery exchange over him being a drag for Democrats
item.description: Hasan Piker clashed with MS NOW's "Clock It" podcast hosts over his anti-Israel stance as Symone Sanders Townsend said she'd tell candidates to disavow him.
item.content:encoded:
Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker clashed with two MS NOW hosts on Wednesday on multiple issues, including his political influence and his anti-Israel stance, as Symone Sanders Townsend told the streamer point-blank she would be telling candidates she worked for to absolutely "disavow" him.

"I used to work campaigns, Hasan, and I have to tell you, if I was a strategist or a consultant or the political director on one of these campaigns, I would absolutely be telling my people to disavow you," Sanders Townsend told Piker in an interview on her "Clock It" podcast, which she co-hosts with Eugene Daniels. "I really would, because we wanna win! We wanna win, and so, like, if you’re not gonna help people win, distance."

Piker acknowledged the disagreement between them as Townsend continued, "I’ve elected people, though. You’ve never elected anybody."

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Piker also maintained his view that Israel is worse than Hamas, though he acknowledged it was a provocative statement. "I do believe that," he said.

"Is Hamas a religious fundamentalist operation that have engaged in violent actions? Of course they have, absolutely," Piker continued. "But that violence is directly born out of, and even that repression is directly born out of, the conditions brought about by the occupation that's been going on for 80 plus years."

Daniels pressed the Twitch streamer on whether he understood that it sounded like he was endorsing violence by making that argument.

"Do you understand that that's how people hear it? And is that what you are endorsing?" Daniels asked.

"So this, again, goes back to the same — this goes back to the same dynamic, right?" Piker said. "Structural violence and state violence is oftentimes made to be invisible. So when Israel as a state is operating its normal state functions, and sometimes it can come across as excessive, right? It's not seen as violent." 

"It's no different than when people protest against police violence and police brutality. The brutality of the police is systemic violence, and therefore it's normalized," he added.

"It's made to be invisible," Piker continued. "Whereas when people protest against the police, that is all of a sudden chaotic, that's all of a sudden violent. It's never violent when the police actually release tear gas on protesters. It's violence if the protesters use leaf blowers to blow that tear gas."

Sanders Townsend jumped in to reject the comparison to protesting the police.

"I'm gonna let Eugene move on, but I just want to note, it sounds like the example that you just gave that the people who are protesting the police are Hamas. And I just would reject that as somebody who has protested the police before, but we can move on," Sanders Townsend said.

HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS

"Symone Sanders Townsend is putting her finger on a real tension for Democrats heading into the midterms," David Scharf, chair of Morrison Cohen’s Government Strategies & Controversies practice, told Fox News Digital. "Hasan Piker gives candidates access to a large, young audience that traditional political media often doesn't reach. But he also gives Republicans a ready-made way to force those candidates to answer for statements they didn't make."

"Every candidate on the record defending him, appearing with him, or refusing to distance themselves from him helps turn him into a campaign issue," he added. 

"In safe blue districts, that may not matter," Scharf said. "In a race as close as Michigan's Senate contest, it can. That's why Sanders Townsend, who has actually run campaigns, is looking at this very differently than Piker is. He's building an audience. She's counting votes."

RASKIN CALLS PIKER’S RHETORIC 'IRRELEVANT DISTRACTION' AFTER THE STREAMER SAID HE'D VOTE FOR HAMAS OVER ISRAEL

Piker insisted during a Friday livestream it was his "God-given" and "constitutionally protected right" to proclaim hatred for America.

During one of his lengthy shows, Piker responded to an attack ad against Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed based on his connection to Piker and his past controversial statements claiming to "hate" America.

"Bro, I hate this country, dude. I hate America," Piker said in clips featured on the ad. "Oh God, I f---ing hate America so much."

Piker argued after showing the clip that it was "clear" that he was angry at "what America as the American government is doing to Americans and to everyone else" but nevertheless defended his right to say he hates the country.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

"Of course, I'm a godd--- American. It is my godd--- God-given and constitutionally protected right to say I hate America if America is actually f---ing over Americans," he said. "You can clip chimp it all day. It doesn't change that. It doesn't change that mentality."

"To present this as like, 'Oh, these guys are real America haters,' as some liberals have been doing on the timeline, as virtually the entirety of the Republican Party is doing, is so f---ing stupid," Piker added.

item.title: Husband and wife get trapped in premier hiking destination; only one of them makes it out alive
item.description: Trapped in deep snow at 7,000 feet in Washington's Enchantments on a hike with her husband, a woman succumbed to the elements as a storm blocked multiple helicopter rescue attempts.
item.content:encoded:
A sudden and powerful storm over Washington state's Cascade Mountains quickly turned a challenging hike into a fight for survival for an Oklahoma couple.

The pair was navigating the rugged "core zone" of the remote Enchantments wilderness when they were engulfed by heavy, deep snow. 

By late afternoon, the freezing, high-elevation conditions brought their trek to a desperate halt.

2 MYSTERY DEATHS AT ZION NATIONAL PARK PROMPT URGENT QUESTIONS ABOUT VISITOR SAFETY

At 5:26 p.m., the husband sent an urgent text to 911. 

He reported to dispatchers that their clothes were soaked through from the storm, and his wife was physically unable to continue moving, according to FOX 13 Seattle.

Help could not reach them in time. 

The stranded hiker, identified as 45-year-old Sybil Claborn of Oklahoma City, succumbed to the extreme elements and died in the snow Sunday.

Before the rescue team reached them, Claborn's husband tried to carry her out but was unable to do so.

They were stranded at an elevation of roughly 7,000 to 8,000 feet, about 8 to 10 miles from the nearest trailheads.

TEEN HIKER'S DISAPPEARANCE ENDS IN TRAGEDY AT NATIONAL PARK WITH KEY QUESTION REMAINING

The situation prompted a frantic rescue effort involving multiple agencies, but the severe weather repeatedly thwarted attempts to reach the couple by air.

The sheriff's office requested a hoist-equipped helicopter at 6:51 p.m., and an Army helicopter launched from Yakima shortly after 8 p.m.

Stormy conditions forced the helicopter to turn back as the husband remained in contact with 911 and reported that Claborn's condition was deteriorating.

A second Army helicopter attempt around 10:50 p.m. was also unsuccessful, while Chelan County Mountain Rescue crews continued toward the couple on foot.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Ground crews finally reached the stranded hikers around 3:30 a.m., finding Claborn dead and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia.

Her husband was warmed inside a tent before he was transported to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment.

Claborn's body was later recovered and taken to the Chelan County Coroner's Office.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Authorities are actively investigating the cause and manner of Claborn's death.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Chelan County Sheriff's Office for more information.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While the tragedy in the Enchantments unfolded amid heavy snow and freezing conditions, other hikers have died this year while battling extreme heat.

Earlier this summer, a 68-year-old French tourist died after attempting to hike to safety after his vehicle became stuck in mud in Death Valley National Park.

A similar tragedy unfolded at the Grand Canyon in June.

That month, an 18-year-old hiker died after developing heat-related symptoms on the park’s Bright Angel Trail, the National Park Service said.

item.title: Fresh activity emerges at Iran’s deeply buried nuclear site as Trump warns Iran not to ‘get cute’
item.description: Satellite imagery reveals Iran added new defenses at Pickaxe Mountain near Natanz as Trump warns Tehran not to "get cute" with the nuclear site.
item.content:encoded:
New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.

The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.

The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.

EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE

The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain.

"We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe," Trump told reporters last week. "I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard."

Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 "Fox & Friends" interview highlighted by the White House, Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew "exactly what’s going on," adding that Washington could "take out Pickaxe" if diplomacy failed.

Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.

TRUMP SAYS US HAS 'MASSIVE' MUNITIONS STOCKPILE, VOWS 'TREASONOUS' LEAKERS BEING HUNTED DOWN

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.

"The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow," Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.

"Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out," he said.

"While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb," Ben Taleblu added. "And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances."

NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT

The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility.

In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was "rapidly moving forward" with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.

The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.

The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations.

CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN

Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-authored Security Council resolution that would have extended for another year, until September 2027, the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. The measure received 11 votes in favor, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.

The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the "snapback" mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.

A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored.

"The snapback sanctions… occurred, the United States and this U.N. Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur," Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. "Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions."

Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.

"The president has been clear, and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution, that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon," Waltz said.

Thursday also brought fresh U.N. scrutiny of both Washington and Tehran. An independent U.N. fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe two U.S. strikes on civilian sites in Iran in February constituted war crimes, while separately concluding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. The mission is investigative rather than judicial, and its findings do not themselves constitute criminal judgments.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Iran U.N. mission for comments but didn’t receive them in time for publication.

item.description: Hurricane charity scams use data brokers and people search sites to target victims before storms even hit, exploiting personal information..

A hurricane-season scammer can start the day with coffee and a spreadsheet. That spreadsheet may hold names, ages, addresses, phone numbers and family details. A scammer might buy that information, pull it from people-search sites or piece it together from public sources.

That means hurricane charity scams can start before a storm even hits. By the time a hurricane dominates the news, a fraudster may already know who could respond to a donation pitch.

September is National Preparedness Month, and this year's theme is "Americans Stand Ready." While FEMA urges you to make an emergency plan and build a kit, scammers are looking for ways to turn a disaster into a payday.

Charity scammers do not have to wait for a disaster to start looking for targets. Data brokers and marketers have spent years collecting information about where people live, what they buy and how they respond to solicitations.

One Justice Department case shows how dangerous that kind of targeting can become. Epsilon Data Management used transactional data and a database covering 100 million U.S. households to identify "responsive buyers." Prosecutors said two executives, Robert Reger and David Lytle, spent about a decade knowingly selling targeted lists to fraudsters.

One client used those lists to defraud more than 218,000 people out of over $23.7 million. More than 12,000 victims got hit more than 20 times. A judge sentenced Reger to 10 years in prison and Lytle to four years. Epsilon also paid $150 million in penalties and victim compensation, with $122 million returned to more than 200,000 victims.

The Epsilon prosecution focused on mass-mailing fraud rather than hurricane charity scams. Still, it shows how personal data and behavioral signals can help fraudsters choose targets before a pitch lands.

Separate FBI data shows the cost of charity fraud. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded 662 charity complaints and $7,907,609 in reported losses in 2025.

A scammer does not need a history of bad donations to target you. Fraudsters can reach people through purchased lists, public records, robocalls and other marketing channels.

James Trankle ran three fake charities, including the "Disabled and Paralyzed Veterans Fund," the "National Breast Cancer Awareness Fund" and the "Children's Leukemia of America Fund." He mailed solicitations to thousands of people and collected more than 1,600 personal checks. Then he used donor banking information to create counterfeit checks. Many victims were older adults. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison.

Travis Peterson ran a six-year scheme using millions of robocalls and other outreach to solicit donations for sham veterans' charities. Prosecutors said he often targeted senior citizens. A judge sentenced him to 41 months in prison and ordered him to pay $541,032.10 in restitution.

These cases show why an unexpected charity pitch deserves a closer look, especially when the caller already knows personal details about you.

MINNESOTA NONPROFIT ACCUSED OF SIPHONING $6.5M TO FUND VEGAS TRIPS, LUXURY CARS, PRIVATE LIQUOR STORE

Natural disasters create urgency and confusion while bringing out people's desire to help. Scammers know that. After Hurricane Helene, FEMA warned that thieves may try to use stolen names, addresses and Social Security numbers to apply for assistance in other people's names. FEMA also warned residents to be alert for impostors posing as inspectors or disaster workers.

The FTC has warned that scammers quickly exploit weather emergencies with fake charities and copycat organizations. Some imitate real charity names or create websites that appear tied to a disaster.

Meanwhile, the Atlantic hurricane season runs through November 30, and NOAA identifies September 10 as the climatological peak. That puts National Preparedness Month right in the middle of the busiest part of the season. You can still be generous. The key is slowing down long enough to verify who wants your money and taking a few steps to protect yourself before you donate.

Look it up on Charity Navigator, BBB Wise Giving Alliance at Give.org, CharityWatch or the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search. Avoid links in unexpected texts or emails. Instead, go directly to the charity's official website.

The FTC warns that scammers may insist on cash, gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency. If you donate, a credit card or check gives you more protection and a clearer paper trail.

A demand to donate immediately should make you stop and verify the organization before sending money. Legitimate charities will give you time to research them and decide whether you want to give.

Scammers may use names that sound like established charities or web addresses that differ by only a few characters. Before donating, check the spelling of the charity's name and make sure you are on its official website.

5) Do not trust donation links in texts, emails or social media posts

A donation request can look convincing even when it comes from a compromised account or impersonates a real charity. Do not assume a fundraiser is legitimate because a friend shared it. Go directly to the charity's official website instead of clicking the donation link and use strong antivirus software to help protect you from malicious links, phishing sites and malware that may be hiding behind fraudulent donation requests.

Review your credit card or bank statement after making a donation. Confirm that you were charged only the amount you approved and check that you were not signed up for recurring donations you did not intend to make. Keep the receipt or confirmation for your records.

If something feels wrong, report it. File a report with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or the FBI at ic3.gov. You can also call the AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline at 877-908-3360.

Verifying every charity request helps, but your personal information may already be available through data brokers and people-search sites. Removing that data can make it harder for scammers to build a detailed profile around you and use personal details to make a pitch seem believable.

item.title: Rand Paul clashes with fellow Republican over AI 'kill switch' as Senate grapples with 'Terminator' fears
item.description: Congress remains gridlocked on AI regulation after Sen. John Kennedy's kill switch bill was blocked and fears grow over rogue AI acting on its own.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., was readying a long-shot attempt at regulating an industry that has, in recent weeks, spurred fears and anxiety about human annihilation.

He planned to ram through his bill, which would require artificial intelligence (AI) companies to have a kill switch for rogue AI, on the Senate floor. But his attempt Wednesday night was blocked by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. 

Kennedy told Fox News Digital he feared there was little desire from Republicans to do anything to regulate AI.

"There's no appetite in my caucus to do anything that I can say," Kennedy said.

HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY

Paul contended the following day that regulating something "so pervasive as AI throughout our economy" would require hearing from people who are involved in the industry and having a debate over the regulatory structure.

"I think it would be crazy to get on the floor one day and regulate an entire industry," Paul told reporters.

Still, the anxiety over the unfettered evolution of AI has spread like wildfire after reports that rogue bots began acting on their own, but it's an issue that Congress has had years to address.

Three years ago, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who was then leading the Senate when Democrats had control under former President Joe Biden, met with lawmakers and Big Tech CEOs to sketch out an AI roadmap. Since then, Congress hasn’t taken legislative action to add guardrails to AI development.

Now, with fears ramping up that AI could wipe out humanity in a decade, and with reports of rogue AI agents scheming privately and attacking other AI, lawmakers are again taking notice.

AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE

But some wonder whether this time Congress will take action to regulate AI, or if it’s turning a growing problem into another political issue to be debated and ignored.

"It's already a political issue," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital. "Donald Trump has said it's not a problem, and that is like a dead weight loss on every one of the Republican senators or representatives.

"Thus far, the courage they have demonstrated in standing up to Donald Trump on anything has been somewhere around zero."

Warren had just left a closed-door meeting led by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who has pushed for a ban on superintelligent AI, held with lawmakers and with AI experts Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI"; physicist Max Tegmark; and Ajeya Cotra.

"There is now a growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating technology that human beings cannot control," Sanders told reporters. "And I'm happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be done."

One of the points the experts impressed on lawmakers was that, at the very least, a kill switch should be implemented to deactivate rogue AI. Kennedy was the lone Republican to attend that meeting.

"I'm just saying they have to have a kill switch to turn the son of a b---- off if it goes wrong," Kennedy said. "This doesn't put government in charge in any way. It doesn't affect innovation. It just says, 'If you're gonna sell this thing in America that has the potential to turn into an independent species, like the 'Terminator,’ you've got to have a way to shut it down immediately, as soon as you discover that.'"

TRUMP-BACKED CRYPTO BILL FAILS TO LAUNCH AS DEMS, REPUBLICANS UNITE TO BLOCK IT

But there have been Republicans, like Kennedy, who want to regulate AI sooner rather than later.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been pushing his regulatory bill alongside Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., since 2023. But Thune argued to Fox News Digital that it was Democrats standing in the way.

"I think the Democrats, in my view, clearly are trying to politicize this. I mean, all the rhetoric around it and everything else, and stuff like that. But you know, the truth is, the bill, which we have, that addresses the AI issue, which we worked on for a long time, which actually passed the Commerce Committee in 2024, is available with modifications and updates. It reflects what's happened since the last time they passed it in our committee.

"The obstacle to getting it up and going and getting it filed is Democrats," he continued. "So, if they're looking for a legislative vehicle, there is one out there."

Meanwhile, Warren said she could see herself supporting a kill switch, but that Hinton made the case that the switch would need a human to flip it, "and a smart AI will persuade a human being not to do it."

"They will create enough evidence, enough of a narrative, that no one will ever throw the kill switch," Warren said. "Which is back to the point I was raising. So, where are the places that you act?"

She argued that Congress needed to find the "pinch points" where humans could still have agency to stop rogue AI. But, for now, there wasn’t a real desire to find a new regulatory and enforcement tool to do so.

"There are things we say are illegal. We have a mechanism for how to enforce the laws that say, ‘Don't do that,’" Warren said. "It's not perfect, but we have it. We need a whole new enforcement device now, and nobody seems to be thinking through what that looks like."

item.title: 'Reacher' star Alan Ritchson exposes alleged extortion plot that sparked suicide attempt
item.description: Alan Ritchson says an alleged blackmail threat at Cannes left him battling depression and uncertainty before a suicide attempt in his mid-30s.
item.content:encoded:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by dialing 988.

Alan Ritchson is sharing an intensely personal account of a period when he says his life began to unravel.

The "Reacher" star said a former business partner threatened to accuse him of rape if he refused to meet her at a hotel in Cannes, France – an alleged threat he says left him overwhelmed by uncertainty and depression.

"I'm a suicide survivor," he said during a recent appearance at FAN EXPO Canada.

item.title: Eva Shockey says women don't have to abandon their femininity to belong in the outdoors
item.description: Eva Shockey reveals the hunting community's pushback she faced for looking feminine and why she refused to change who she is to fit the mold.
item.content:encoded:
Eva Shockey never thought becoming a hunter should require giving up the other parts of herself.

Apparently, plenty of people disagreed.

Shockey, one of the most recognizable women in the outdoor industry, told OutKick's Tomi Lahren that she has faced pushback from within the hunting community almost from the moment she entered it — including criticism for something as simple as wanting to look feminine while doing it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"Pretty much everything I've done in the hunting community, there's been pushback since day one," Shockey said during an appearance on "Tomi Lahren is Fearless." "It's never been where everyone's like, 'Yeah, she's doing it right.' Like, it's just never been like that."

But fitting neatly into someone else's idea of what a hunter should look like was never particularly appealing to her.

Shockey grew up in a hunting family as the daughter of legendary outdoorsman Jim Shockey, but she didn't immediately follow her dad into the field. In fact, one of the things that kept her away from hunting when she was younger was that she didn't see women who looked or lived like her doing it.

When she eventually began hunting herself, she wasn't interested in trading one identity for another.

"I didn't hunt because I didn't know you could be this — have hair and makeup and care about your nails being done — and also love to hunt," she said. "I love being in the mountains. I love hiking. I love wearing camo, but I also like still looking feminine."

Her solution was pretty simple: Don't choose.

"If I'm gonna hunt, I'm still me," Shockey said. "I'm not gonna change who I am because I want to go hunting."

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

That became a defining part of her message as her profile grew over the years.

Shockey came into the outdoor industry at a time when hunting media was still overwhelmingly male. She started on television alongside her father before social media opened the door for women and other newcomers to find outdoor personalities who looked more like them.

She is quick to point out that she didn't create the movement toward more women hunting.

"I got to really ride the wave of a big change in more women starting to hunt," Shockey said. "It wasn't me personally. Like, no, I'm not going to take all that credit. There was a bunch of other women before me. I just got to be a bit of a face of it and represent a lot of women through those last 15 years or so."

Still, she has seen the change firsthand.

Shockey believes social media, for all its faults, has made the outdoor world far more accessible to girls who might otherwise grow up believing hunting simply isn't something women do.

"If young girls want to see someone shooting a bow or they live out in the country and they've never seen a girl hunt — which was little Eva back in the day — they can open social and see people doing what they want to do," she said.

And they don't all have to look the same.

"I'm by no means everybody's style," Shockey said. "Not everyone wants to see someone with, like, hair and makeup done. But there's lots."

That's precisely the point.

For Shockey, expanding hunting isn't about replacing one stereotype with another. It's about showing women that they don't have to adopt a particular personality, appearance or identity before they're allowed to participate.

CHASE BRISCOE SAYS DEER HUNTING GIVES HIM A BIGGER RUSH THAN DRIVING 200 MPH IN NASCAR

Over the years, she said, that message has come back to her directly.

"I had a lot of girls, thousands and thousands of girls over the years, come up to me with basically relaying that to me," Shockey said. "Like, 'I'm so glad you said that we could hunt and not be embarrassed of who we are or what we look like or where we're from or whatever that looks like.'"

And it isn't necessarily about makeup or femininity.

"Maybe it's not hair and makeup," she said. "It's just you want to be who you are and still enjoy hunting. You don't have to transition into a hunter and leave everything else out. Like, we all have more elements than that."

Shockey also believes the broader culture has moved closer to the outdoor lifestyle in recent years. More people, she said, are showing interest in gardening, sourcing their own food, hunting and generally reconnecting with where food comes from.

"It's changed a lot in the last five years," she said. "I think people are very interested in that lifestyle, and they're very interested in growing things themselves, hunting things themselves."

Rather than policing exactly how deeply someone participates, Shockey would rather see that curiosity encouraged.

"The things that I believe so strongly in — like the outdoor life, the hunting, the gardens, the healthy food for your family, the fresh air, all that — I believe it's such a great thing," she said. "Even if they're doing 10% of it, that's 10% better than not doing it."

And for Shockey, that may be the bigger win.

Not everyone has to become a hardcore hunter. But if seeing women with different personalities, interests and backgrounds makes the outdoors feel a little less foreign — and a little more accessible — then she’s certainly done her job.

item.title: Minnesota's anti-ICE aid fund becomes latest casualty of state's embarrassing fraud problem
item.description: Hennepin County paid out $500,000 in grants before shutting down a $2 million program tied to Operation Metro Surge due to overwhelming fraud.
item.content:encoded:
A program designed to assist businesses impacted by the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts in Minnesota has been shut down following widespread fraud concerns, according to local news reports.

The board of Hennepin County in Minnesota, home to Minneapolis, approved $2 million in funding for local businesses impacted by Operation Metro Surge — a large-scale immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota launched in December 2025. The county received roughly 300 applications and ultimately distributed about $500,000 to 82 applicants, while more than 200 applications were flagged for potential fraud, according to local reports.

"The fact that people, after all this fraud, felt that they could apply and get away with it, I think it's a problem because clearly there's no fear out there," Hennepin County Commissioner Jeff Lunde said, according to Kare 11. "Until we get it where people fear things, then they're gonna keep doing it."

EMMER SAYS MN FRAUD RAIDS SEND ‘CRYSTAL CLEAR’ MESSAGE AFTER FEDS HIT DOZENS OF SITES

Much of President Donald Trump’s rhetoric surrounding illegal immigration in Minnesota has been targeted at the state’s Somali population amid reports of widespread fraud.

Members of Minnesota’s Somali community have been accused, and in some cases convicted, of using non-existent or inactive businesses and nonprofits to siphon money away from government programs intended to help the needy.

FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE'

Similarly, Hennepin County officials reported that many businesses seeking relief funds drafted applications containing false information, seemingly fabricated by AI, that were copied, pasted, and submitted for multiple businesses. Other businesses submitting applications, meanwhile, were found not to exist when county officials made site visits.

"Then at a certain point we're like, 'OK, we're getting declining results on that.' And so we said it's time to stop the program. So we just stopped processing at that point," Lunde, who characterized the applications as overwhelmingly fraudulent, said.

The immigration enforcement operation in the state also drew national attention after U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot by federal agents in Minneapolis in January.

WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT'

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, has acknowledged responsibility for addressing the fraud in his state, saying it is his "responsibility to fix it." He has previously argued that "any amount of fraud is too much and undermines the very programs that do so much to raise our quality of life." 

The governor, however, has pushed back on conservative attempts to pin the fraud primarily on the Somali community in the state. 

"What is not helpful is the president of the United States demonizing an entire community," the governor wrote in a December 2025 op-ed.

Hennepin County and Walz's office did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

item.title: Body of missing hiker found in Olympic National Park thanks to crucial clue
item.description: Neil Gehring left Olympic National Park's Madison Falls Trailhead for an overnight trek and never returned.
item.content:encoded:
The body of a missing 26-year-old hiker in Washington state's Olympic National Park was recovered nearly two weeks after he set out on a backcountry trek, following a crucial break in the search, officials said.

Searchers located Neil Gehring on the northwest slope of Mount Appleton after receiving and analyzing additional cellphone location data, according to the National Park Service.

Search-and-rescue teams recovered Gehring’s body Sunday evening. He was taken to the Clallam County Coroner’s Office at about 8 p.m. on Sept. 13.

MISSING 70-YEAR-OLD HIKER RESCUED AFTER DISAPPEARING FOR A WEEK IN REMOTE NATIONAL PARK

Officials did not release details about the cellphone data or the circumstances of Gehring’s death.

Gehring left the Madison Falls Trailhead on Aug. 31 for what was supposed to be an overnight backcountry trip.

His permit showed that he planned to make a cross-country trek from Boulder Lake to Appleton Pass before returning to the trailhead on Sept. 1.

Gehring was reported overdue at 6:30 a.m. the next morning, prompting an immediate search.

MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE

For the next 10 days, teams searched his expected route from the air and ground, using drones and dogs as part of the effort.

By Sept. 11, the park announced it was changing tactics after the searches failed to locate Gehring. Teams would instead focus on finding new clues that could help narrow the search.

Investigators also asked anyone who had been in the area or had information about Gehring’s whereabouts to come forward.

Two days later, searchers found Gehring after receiving and analyzing the additional cellphone location data.

Olympic National Park thanked the search-and-rescue teams that volunteered to help with the effort.

NPS said no additional information was available at this time.

item.description: Abdul El-Sayed's 2011 comments reveal his long-standing vision for Medicare-for-all and making healthcare more expensive for wealthier patients.
item.content:encoded:
Over a decade before becoming the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged that his vision for healthcare would require different costs for patients depending on wealth status.

"We’re actually just going to give other people access to what you have and make yours more expensive. We’re not asking you to lose access. We’re just making yours more expensive. And not that much so, in fact. We’re making it marginally more expensive," El-Sayed said in a 2011 appearance on the "Sense and Sustainability" podcast.

His resurfaced comments, made as part of a program on inequalities in healthcare, reveal El-Sayed’s long-standing thinking behind his proposed policy changes.

DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE

Fifteen years later, El-Sayed has made an expansion of healthcare in the U.S. a key part of his platform as he wages a bid to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich.

In particular, he has championed Medicare-for-all, an expansion of the federal program that covers healthcare costs for U.S. citizens over the age of 65 and for some younger recipients with long-term disabilities.

El-Sayed’s plan would expand public coverage for everyone, regardless of income, age or job.

"Medicare-for-all means no premium, no co-pay, no deductible. Doesn’t matter if you get a job, lose a job, turn 26, turn 65, get married, get divorced — it is there for you," El-Sayed said in a post to X earlier this year.

Skeptics of the plan argue it is too expensive and does little to address existing inefficiencies in the American healthcare system.

In 2019, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., took to the Senate floor to blast the idea, calling it a straitjacket solution that would undermine health care quality.

LIZ PEEK: MICHIGAN CAN STOP THE SOCIALIST FEVER RAGE — OR WATCH IT SWALLOW THE SENATE

"The [Congressional Budget Office] projects in its report on a single-payer plan that government spending on health care would increase substantially. They go on to say to cover the massive cost of government-run care, income taxes would have to at least double. Income taxes, American families — at least double," Barrasso said.

"Mark my words, Medicare-for-all would soon become Medicare for none."

Despite its hefty price tag, in El-Sayed’s view, the plan is key to ensuring equality of outcomes, even if individual patients are charged differently. He expounded on his design in the 2011 interview.

"We wouldn’t necessarily be ‘stealing from the rich to give to the poor’ in the U.S. because the rich will always have the ability to pay for the care that they need," El-Sayed said.

"The argument would be that everyone’s premiums would go up a little bit. But for the people who actually have premiums now, what they’re losing in terms of the added costs on their health plans are more manageable to them than is the absolute lack of access to healthcare among the people that don’t have it now."

El-Sayed argued that his vision would make costs only marginally more expensive for top earners.

SOCIALISM'S WAR ON SUCCESS HAS A NEW CHAMPION — AND HE’S RUNNING FOR SENATE IN MICHIGAN

His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether it could expand on the costs of El-Sayed’s vision. Having cleared the Democratic primary in Michigan, El-Sayed will face Republican challenger Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the state's Nov. 3 general election.
